passage: When I was ten, I lost something almost every day. I'm Shankar. My water bottle, my library book, the permission slip for the zoo trip. Amma would sigh, "Again?" and I'd feel hot and ashamed, like I was bad. But I wasn't lazy. Some nights I'd get an idea and build a whole volcano model till midnight, totally focused. Then I'd forget where I put my shoes. One Sunday Amma stopped scolding. She stuck a picture checklist on the door: bottle, bag, book, tiffin, with little drawings. Every morning I touched each picture before leaving. I still forgot sometimes, but much less. And Amma said "Good job" more than "Again?"

qa.q: What did Amma stick on the door?
qa.a: A picture checklist: bottle, bag, book, tiffin, with little drawings.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when Amma said "Again?"
qa.a: Shankar felt hot and ashamed, as if being forgetful meant being bad.

qa.q: Why did the checklist work better than scolding?
qa.a: It gave a simple visual routine to follow each morning, so Shankar forgot less and heard more praise than reminders.

qa.q: How might Amma feel saying "Good job" more often?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and happier, glad the checklist replaced daily frustration.

grounding: Shows a child who forgets things and works in bursts when interested, feels bad about reminders, and is helped by a visual checklist rather than scolding.

passage: In Istanbul, Camila, sixteen, had her exam timetable taped above her desk: blue for chemistry, green for history, every hour colour-coded. Then an earthquake drill and a power cut wiped out two whole days of study. On the second night she sat up till two, copying notes by phone torchlight, furious with herself. "I'm so behind. I don't deserve a break." Her friend Zeynep came over with simit and found her red-eyed. "You're the most disciplined person I know. But you're punishing yourself for a power cut." Camila laughed shakily. Zeynep helped her redraw the week with two catch-up slots and one free evening. That night, Camila slept eight hours, and felt guilty only for about ten minutes.

qa.q: What wiped out two days of Camila's study?
qa.a: An earthquake drill and a power cut.

qa.q: How did Camila feel about losing two days?
qa.a: She felt guilty and furious with herself, as if she didn't deserve a break.

qa.q: What did Zeynep help Camila do?
qa.a: Zeynep helped her redraw the timetable with catch-up slots and a free evening, instead of punishing herself.

qa.q: How does Zeynep see Camila's discipline?
qa.a: Zeynep sees it as a real strength, but worries it has turned into self-punishment.

grounding: Shows a disciplined teenager who colour-codes her study and feels guilty when life interrupts, and a friend helping her see rigid plans have become self-punishment.

passage: Last year, I finally learnt how to plan without breaking myself. I'm Ishita. In Class 10 my friend Jasleen and I both made huge timetables. Jasleen followed hers perfectly, pulling all-nighters, until she got sick a week before the boards. I built mine differently. Every Wednesday evening was blank, a buffer. Sunday afternoons were off. Lights out at ten-thirty, no matter what. When my cousin's wedding took two days in February, I didn't panic. I looked at what I'd missed, moved it into the buffers and carried on. A missed day just told me I'd planned too tight. I didn't top the class, but I studied steadily every week, and I walked into the exams rested.

qa.q: What did Ishita leave blank every Wednesday evening?
qa.a: A buffer, left blank.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when the wedding took two days?
qa.a: Ishita felt calm, not panicked, seeing the missed days as something to adjust for.

qa.q: What makes Ishita's plan a wise balance of effort and rest?
qa.a: It builds in slack, protects sleep, treats a missed day as information and values consistency over perfection.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel comparing her boards preparation with Ishita's?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel exhausted and regretful, having burned out after all-nighters while Ishita stayed rested.

grounding: Shows a teenager who keeps a plan with slack, treats a missed day as information, values consistency over perfection and makes sleep part of the plan.

passage: Tushar, twenty, never booked anything early. At his Bengaluru college, friends joked he decided lunch at the counter. But when the chief guest for the fest cancelled an hour before the opening, Tushar was the one who calmly rang an alumni band, rearranged the stage order and had the crowd singing in twenty minutes. Two weeks later, though, he forgot the group project deadline entirely. Sonali, his partner, was furious. "Your flexibility is great, but I can't be your calendar." Tushar felt embarrassed. That evening they agreed on two anchors: a shared calendar with alerts for every deadline, and a check-in every Monday at nine. He still decided lunch at the counter. But he never missed another submission.

qa.q: What did Tushar arrange when the chief guest cancelled?
qa.a: He rang an alumni band, rearranged the stage order and had the crowd singing in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when Sonali got angry about the deadline?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, realising his style had let her down.

qa.q: What anchors did they agree on, and why do they help?
qa.a: A shared calendar with deadline alerts and a Monday check-in, so Tushar's flexibility doesn't break shared commitments.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about carrying the deadlines alone?
qa.a: Sonali felt frustrated and angry, refusing to be Tushar's calendar.

grounding: Shows a young adult who adapts well in changing situations but needs deliberate anchors like shared calendars for deadlines and commitments.

subtype: Living with a very careful partner or roommate [Receiver]
passage:
Warden's note, women's hostel, Room 12.
Lavanya came to see me this week, upset. Her roommate, Indu, is extremely orderly: she pays the electricity share on the first of every month, keeps a chore chart and never misses a turn. Lavanya said she's grateful; she has never once worried about bills. But Indu also refolds Lavanya's towels, moves her books back "to the right shelf" and sighs when her bed isn't made. Lavanya said she'd been quietly fuming for weeks.
I suggested she say it plainly. On Thursday she told Indu, "Bills and the chore chart are real needs, and I'm with you. How my shelf looks is your preference, not a need." Indu was quiet, then agreed. Lavanya says the room feels lighter. — Hostel warden

qa.q: When does Indu pay the electricity share?
qa.a: On the first of every month.

qa.q: How had Lavanya been feeling about Indu's corrections?
qa.a: She felt grateful for the order but also watched and resentful, quietly fuming for weeks.

qa.q: What did Lavanya say that eased the tension?
qa.a: She plainly separated real needs, like bills and chores, from Indu's preferences, like how shelves look.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when Lavanya spoke to her?
qa.a: Indu may have felt surprised and a little stung at first, then relieved to know what mattered, since she agreed.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels safe with her orderly roommate's care of bills and chores but also watched, and who plainly separates needs from preferences.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,
I've wanted to write this for a while. On our team, you're the one who never misses a deadline. You remembered the client's name in Tuesday's call when none of us did. You quietly fixed the broken links in the report at eleven at night. We all trust you completely.
But I've noticed something. Every time something goes wrong, we say, "Ask Ujjwal." Nobody says thank you. Last week you looked grey and exhausted, and you snapped at the printer, which isn't like you.
So, thank you. Truly. And I've asked Priya to split the reporting work so you're not the only safety net. I'll bring it up at Monday's meeting too.
Aadhya

qa.q: What did Ujjwal remember in Tuesday's call?
qa.a: The client's name.

qa.q: How does Aadhya feel about how the team treats Ujjwal?
qa.a: Aadhya feels grateful to Ujjwal but uneasy and concerned that the team leans on Ujjwal without thanks.

qa.q: What steps does Aadhya take to help?
qa.a: Aadhya thanks Ujjwal, asks Priya to split the reporting work and plans to raise it at Monday's meeting.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ujjwal may feel seen and appreciated, and relieved that someone noticed the exhaustion.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a reliable teammate who delivers on time and fixes gaps, over-relied on and unthanked, and acting before burnout.

passage: At the Sunday vegetable market in Mumbai, Santosh, two, waved at everyone from his father's hip. "Hi! Hi!" The fish seller waved back and Santosh shrieked with joy. He wriggled down to sit beside the vendor's little girl and poked her toy lorry, laughing loudly. When he grabbed it, Vishal, his father, knelt. "Soft hands. Ask first." Santosh let go. At home in the quiet flat, he drooped and whined until the neighbour's children came over.

qa.q: Who waved back at Santosh first?
qa.a: The fish seller.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel at the busy market?
qa.a: He felt excited and joyful, shrieking and laughing around all the people.

qa.q: What did Vishal do when Santosh grabbed the toy?
qa.a: He knelt and taught a gentle limit, saying "Soft hands. Ask first."

qa.q: How might the vendor's little girl have felt when Santosh grabbed her lorry?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised or upset, though Santosh let go once his father stepped in.

grounding: Shows a social toddler who waves at strangers, seeks others to play beside and gets loud, gaining energy around people, with an adult teaching gentle limits.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: At the Lucknow Sunday market, Ojas, five, chatted to every vendor about mangoes, dogs and his new tooth. His twin, Mitali, held her father's finger and stared at her sandals. "Say hello to Uncle, Mitali," Uday urged. She shrank behind him. Uday felt pulled two ways and a little frustrated. Then he remembered her silence after last week's party. He let Ojas chat with the banana seller and walked Mitali to the quiet end of the market, where she silently pointed out three pigeons and a cat. Riding home, Ojas talked nonstop; Mitali leaned on her father, content.

qa.q: What did Ojas chat to vendors about?
qa.a: Mangoes, dogs and his new tooth.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when Mitali shrank behind him?
qa.a: He felt pulled two ways and a little frustrated, trying to meet both children's needs at once.

qa.q: What did Uday do that respected both children?
qa.a: He let Ojas chat with the banana seller and took Mitali to a quiet spot, giving each a different kind of attention.

qa.q: How might Mitali feel leaning on her father on the way home?
qa.a: Mitali may feel safe and content, understood without being pushed to talk.

grounding: Shows a parent of a chatty child and a quiet child, feeling pulled between them, giving each a different kind of attention instead of forcing sameness.

passage: In their Delhi colony, Tenzin, ten, had organised a cricket team, a kite club and a treasure hunt, all in one summer. Everyone came to his door. But in class silent reading felt like torture; he tapped his pencil, whispered jokes and got shushed twice. At break he rushed up to Swati, who was sitting alone with a book. "Come on, we need a fielder!" She shook her head. He kept talking, about the match, the new ball, a funny video. Swati turned a page, her lips tight. Tenzin finally noticed. "You want to read, right?" She nodded. "Sorry. I'll save you a turn after lunch." Swati smiled for the first time that day.

qa.q: How many activities did Tenzin organise that summer?
qa.a: Three: a cricket team, a kite club and a treasure hunt.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel during silent reading?
qa.a: He felt restless and bored, tapping his pencil and whispering jokes.

qa.q: What did Tenzin learn to do with Swati?
qa.a: He noticed her quiet cue, her tight lips, asked what she wanted and gave her space, offering a turn later.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt while Tenzin kept talking?
qa.a: Swati probably felt crowded and a bit irritated, wanting quiet time with her book.

grounding: Shows a talkative child who leads games and is restless during silent work, energised by company but at first missing a friend's quiet cue for space.

passage: At her cousin's wedding, the generator failed during the sangeet and the hall went dark and even noisier. Vidya, nine, stood by the wall and watched while the other children screamed and ran around with phone torches. She didn't join at first. She noticed who was bossy, who was kind. Then her cousin Chinmay, her one close friend in the family, came to stand beside her. "Want to hold the torch together?" They made shadow animals on the wall for an hour, laughing. By ten she was worn out. While the dancing went on, she slipped up to the terrace with a shawl and sat alone under the stars. When her mother came up, worried, Vidya smiled. "I'm happy, Ma. I just need quiet now."

qa.q: What did Vidya and Chinmay make on the wall?
qa.a: Shadow animals.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel by ten o'clock?
qa.a: She felt tired and drained after the busy evening, though still happy.

qa.q: Why was going to the terrace a good choice for Vidya?
qa.a: Quiet time alone helped her recover her energy after a noisy, crowded party.

qa.q: How might Vidya's mother have felt finding her on the terrace?
qa.a: She may have been worried at first, then reassured when Vidya said she was happy and just needed quiet.

grounding: Shows a quiet child who watches a new group before joining, prefers one close friend and recovers from a busy party through solitude, not unhappiness, despite a power failure.
